Part 2: Advanced RAG Techniques - Layer by Layer
If you missed Part 1: RAG Metrics and When to Use Them, go check it out first - because knowing how to measure flaws is step one. Now, let’s talk about fixing them.
In Part 1, we explored RAG metrics - precision, recall, coverage, faithfulness, answerability - and how to track them. But metrics alone don’t make your system stronger. They just tell you where it’s weak.
👉 In Part 2, we move from diagnosis to treatment. RAG has five natural layers, and each layer comes with techniques designed to solve specific failure modes. Stack them together, and you build a pipeline that’s resistant to hallucinations and robust in production.
Let’s start the film now!!
RAG has 5 natural layers where techniques can be applied:
Each layer solves specific failure modes. The stronger your pipeline at each layer, the more hallucination-resistant your system.
Layer 1: Pre-Retrieval - Smart Query Processing
Problems solved: Vague queries, ambiguous terms, vocabulary mismatches, multi-aspect questions.
Why it matters: Queries from real users are often messy. “How do I fix my thing?” doesn’t tell the retriever what the customer’s problem is. Pre-retrieval techniques clean up the query before it ever hits the database.
HyDE - Hypothetical Document Embeddings
Instead of embedding the raw query, ask the LLM to generate a hypothetical answer, then embed that hypothetical answer.
Mechanism:
Why it works:
•
Short query (“How do I reset my login?”) is far from a 150-token help article in the embedding space
•
A hypothetical answer is already written in the same style/length as real articles
•
The embedding of the hypothetical answer is much closer to real articles
Practical impact: +5–15% Recall@K improvement on short, ambiguous queries.
Trade-off: Requires one extra LLM call (the hypothetical generation). Acceptable since you’re trading for better retrieval.
When to use:
•
Short user queries (< 10 words)
•
Knowledge bases with long, detailed articles
•
When basic retrieval underperforms
Query Decomposition: Breaking Complex Questions into Sub-queries
Many real questions span multiple topics. Instead of throwing one complex query at the retriever, break it into sub-queries, retrieve for each, merge results.
Real example: Customer asks:
"I'm a new user with a team of 5. What plan should I choose, and can I pay annually?"
Decomposed into:
•
Sub-query 1: “New user pricing, multi-seat plans”
•
Sub-query 2: “Team account setup, 5 users”
•
Sub-query 3: “Annual billing, payment options”
Retrieval flow:
Each sub-query → retrieve top 5 articles separately ↓ Merge results using RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion): - Article A ranked #2 in sub-query 1, #5 in sub-query 3 - Article B ranked #1 in sub-query 3, not in others - etc. ↓ Final ranking: AB, AC, BD... (accounts for all perspectives)
RRF formula:
RRF(d) = Σ (1 / (k + rank(d, q))) where k=60 (smoothing constant)
Impact: +20–30% improvement on multi-faceted queries.
When to use:
•
Questions with multiple AND conditions
•
Queries that naturally split into categories
•
When users are known to ask complex questions
Query Expansion via Pseudo-Relevance Feedback (PRF)
Why we need PRF?
•
Vocabulary mismatch: Users often phrase queries differently than how documents are written. For example, “payment methods” vs. “billing setup.” Without expansion, the retrieval engine may miss relevant docs.
•
Domain-specific jargon: In specialized fields (finance, medicine, law), the right keywords matter. PRF helps bridge the gap by pulling in domain terms from retrieved docs.
•
Boosting recall: If the initial query is too narrow, PRF broadens it with related terms, increasing the chance of finding all relevant documents.
How it works?
Assume the top-1 retrieved document is relevant. Extract its keywords, add them to the original query, re-retrieve with the expanded query.
Process:
Original query: "payment methods" ↓ Retrieve top 1: Article about "Billing Setup" ↓ Extract keywords: ["billing", "invoice", "card", "invoice_payment", "auto_billing"] ↓ Expanded query: "payment methods billing invoice card auto_billing" ↓ Re-retrieve with expanded query ↓ Better results because we now include relevant terminology
Assumption: Top-1 is correct and contains good vocabulary. Works 70–80% of the time but fails if top-1 is wrong (then you retrieve garbage-related documents).
Practical strategy: Use as optional fallback rather than default. If initial retrieval scores are low, try expansion.
When to use:
•
Queries with poor recall using basic methods
•
When you have domain-specific vocabulary mismatch.
Synonym & Ontology Expansion
Why need it?
In specialized domains, customers use different words for the same thing. Maintain a synonym map and expand queries with known synonyms.
Real example (SaaS billing domain):
"pricing tiers" → also expand for: ["plans", "subscription levels", "packages", "pricing levels"] "refund" → also expand for: ["reimbursement", "chargeback", "credit", "reversal"] "SSO" → also expand for: ["single sign-on", "federated login", "SAML", "OAuth"]
Application:
Original query: "how do I set up SSO?" ↓ Expanded query: "how do I set up SSO, single sign-on, federated login, SAML, OAuth?" ↓ Retriever has many more chances to find relevant docs
Maintenance burden: Someone needs to build and maintain the synonym map. Worth it for mature products.
When to use:
•
Highly specialized domains (healthcare, legal, finance)
•
When you have controlled vocabulary (taxonomy) already
•
Product categories, feature names, compliance terms
Now let’s see layer 2.
Layer 2: Retrieval - Finding the Right Documents
By the time a query reaches the retriever, it’s been cleaned and expanded. Now we retrieve documents using various strategies.
Hybrid Search: Combining BM25 (Sparse) + Dense + RRF
BM25 (full-text search) excels at exact keyword matching but misses semantic similarity. Dense (embedding-based) retrieval catches semantics but misses exact phrases.
Real example:
Query: “Can I change my payment method?”
•
BM25 only: Returns articles with “payment” and “method” in the title. Might miss a help article titled “Updating Your Billing Information” (semantically the same).
•
Dense only: Returns semantically similar articles including some about account security, billing overview, etc. But an article titled “Payment Methods” might rank lower because “method” doesn’t appear in the embedding.
•
Hybrid: Retrieves top-5 from BM25, top-5 from dense, merges via RRF.
RRF merging:
BM25 scores: [doc_A=0.95, doc_B=0.87, doc_C=0.72, ...] Dense scores: [doc_B=0.92, doc_D=0.88, doc_A=0.81, ...] (different ranking!) ↓ RRF combines: doc_B (ranks well in both) → top doc_A (good in both) doc_C, doc_D (good in one)
Impact: Typically 10–20% improvement in Recall@K vs. either method alone.
Production implementation:
•
BM25 from Elasticsearch, Solr, or Milvus
•
Dense from FAISS, Pinecone, or Weaviate
•
Merge via RRF or normalized score combination
Multi-Vector Retrieval: ColBERT and Token-Level Embeddings
Why needed: Traditional dense retrieval compresses a whole doc into one vector, losing fine-grained meaning. ColBERT keeps token-level embeddings, allowing precise matches.
Instead of one embedding per document, compute one embedding per token, then match query tokens to document tokens individually.
Mechanism:
Traditional dense: 1 embedding per document (768 dimensions) ColBERT: embeddings for every token: - Document: 500 tokens → 500 embeddings (768-dim each) - Query: "reset password" → 2 embeddings Score = MaxSim: for each query token, find its best match in document tokens
Formula:
score(query, doc) = Σ_token_in_query max_token_in_doc similarity(token
Real example:
Query: “Can I change my password?”
Document about “Security Settings”: contains “password”, “change”, “login”, “two-factor”, etc.
•
Traditional embedding: might match on “security settings” overall but misses exact terms
•
ColBERT: token “password” matches token “password” (perfect match), token “change” matches token “change” (perfect match) → very high score
Trade-offs:
•
Pro: More expressive - token-level matching captures nuance
•
Con: Storage is 100–500x larger (500 tokens × 768 dimensions per document)
•
Con: Retrieval is slower (many token similarity computations)
When to use: When single-vector retrieval is clearly failing, and you have compute/storage budget.
Ensemble & Multi-Retriever Architectures
No single retriever dominates across all query types. Run multiple retrieval methods in parallel, merge results.
Real example:
Retrieval pipeline: ├─ BM25 (exact keywords) ├─ Dense (semantic) ├─ Knowledge Graph (entity relationships) ├─ Keyword (TF-IDF) └─ Rules (e.g., FAQ → top result)
Merge via RRF + weighted voting: Article retrieved by all 5 methods → highest rank Article retrieved by 3 methods → medium rank Article retrieved by 1 method → lower rank
Impact: Very resilient to failure of any single method.
When to use: High-stakes applications where missing the right document is expensive.
